blocks.text: This article is about the Coquette sub-aesthetic. For the anime "femcel" aesthetic, see Femcel.

Waif, also known as Girlblogger, Female Manipulator, or Femcel, is an internet aesthetic and persona within the Coquette sphere. It revolves around a modern archetype of a young woman who is intelligent, misunderstood, beautiful, and emotionally troubled, often exhibiting self-destructive, toxic, or manipulative tendencies. The imagery of the aesthetic reflects that complex lifestyle, emphasizing both its chaotic nature and its aspirational qualities.

The Waif aesthetic is one of many that developed out of the Heroin Chic trend and its cultural influence over womanhood. Waif draws significant inspiration from the Dark Nymphet, Sadgirl and pro-ana communities. Some of the defining features of this aesthetic are its relation to media about unlikable, flawed female protagonists and a cynical, detached sense of humor (partially inspired by the podcast Red Scare). Waif content is not limited to curated images; it is also heavily conveyed through memes, mood boards, anonymous confessions on the app Whisper, and text posts about users' personal lives.

While it shares visuals with many Coquette-related aesthetics, its unique embrace of controversial values and viewpoints, unashamed portrayal of mental illness, and acceptance of toxic personality traits sets it apart.

The Waif aesthetic has many influences that stem from the 2000s and 2010s, such as Heroin Chic, 2000s fashion culture (see McBling), Nymphet, and Soft Grunge. It is deeply connected to Lobotomy Chic, Pink Pilates Princess and Slavic Doll, as they often all share the same online spaces and cultures.

The visual motifs and philosophy of Waif are a result of many individual trends from 2020 that, when combined, form the aesthetic. Thinness becoming trendy again, Balletcore and Coquette gaining prominence in runway fashion, and Catholicism coming to be known as both cool and subversive among Gen Z are all contributing factors to Waif philosophy. The 2020s has also seen a shifting perspective on engaging with literature as a hobby, where the identity of being a "reader" has become an attractive trait online. In addition, the rise of "girl internet," a trend where young women identify with and label all of their habits as something related to "girls," was also influential, with Waif being both a result and a propellant of the trend.

The Waif aesthetic first appeared circa 2020 through Pinterest, Tumblr, and the Whisper app, later spreading onto Instagram through reposts of content from the other social media sites. In July 2025, the Whisper app was discontinued and removed from the Apple App and Google Play Stores, so many of the posts that originated this aesthetic are either reposted on other sites, imitated in format, or lost to time. On Tumblr, these photos are spread through mass-tagging using Waif-related tags, such as "waifspo," "this is what makes us girls," "hell is a teenage girl," "girlblogging," and more.

The term "waif" has two relevant definitions in the Merriam-Webster Dictionary: "1a: a stray person or animal, especially a homeless child. 2: an extremely thin and usually young woman." This word was chosen by the community as a way to get around Tumblr and Pinterest censorship. When these sites banned "thinspo" (posts used to inspire users to continue to restrict their food intake) and related pro-ana tags, the community shifted towards tags such as "waifspo," which is where the name of the aesthetic originates. Many women who are currently active in the Girlblogging community will still use "waif" and "waifspo" as tags beneath their posts, even if the post itself isn't about body image.

In around 2022, a print and digital publication called Delude Magazine was created by Ciggy Spencer (Editor-in-Chief) and Jana Surkova (Creative Director), directly emerging from the Waif internet aesthetic. It embraces "delusional girl" culture and features writings, essays, journal entries, photo shoots and quizzes by and for people within the Waif sphere. In July 2024, CharliXCX released the album brat, and on it, she included the song "Mean Girls," which described a Girlblogger/Waif-type with words like "problematic," "anorexic," "coquettish," and "intelligent" -- this song was written about podcaster Dasha Nekrasova, a Waif icon and long-time trailblazer for the aesthetic. As a result, "Mean Girls" made Waif subculture more widely known to internet-users who had previously never encountered it before.

Note: Because the claims may be interpreted as harsh, there is a gallery with image evidence supporting the claims made here. As the primary source of Waif posts is the Whisper app, a good amount of documentation of/for the aesthetic is in the text-on-photo format.

The Waif community largely preoccupies itself with femininity in all aspects: the experiences, joys, and tragedies of being a feminine teenager and young adult (mostly geared towards white and middle to upper-middle class girls, though the Trailer Park Princess trope is also romanticized), as well as the difficulties of teendom and womanhood. Text posts often vent about the insecurities and uncertainties women face throughout life. Alongside this, many posts celebrate the joys of girlhood, such as fashion, female friendships, and male attention (both craving and rejecting it).

Appearance is one of the primary fixations of this community; this aesthetic is overtly engrossed with becoming beautiful through weight loss, a curated personal style, and by outwardly projecting a desirable, confident attitude, even if it's a facade. Partially, this is because they recognize the social rewards for doing so. Some posts indicate that many Waifs believe they will acquire the things they desire most (such as money, social status, and self-love) through focusing on their appearance. Contrarily, other Waif posts assert that this interest is purely superficial, and that their sense of self entirely depends on how beautiful they are, nothing more and nothing less.

Despite partying and drug use having a large presence in this aesthetic, academic success, literature and schooling are also romanticized (often as a way to cope with the stress of school and being a high-achiever). Pretentiousness is celebrated, and high literature, poetry, and philosophy are used to seem intellectual, explore their life experience, and as topics of conversation. Many posts involve snippets of philosophical thoughts super-imposed over images. Rumination over relations of the self to others, the meaning of life, and concepts such as the erotic grotesque, the myth of Sisyphus, and the Madonna-Whore complex are common.

Waif subculture is fascinated by religion and the esoteric, specifically with Catholicism. Users in the community often relate to female saints -- a Waif, through her intellectualism, lack of human connection, and inner turmoil, can sympathize with a saints' disconnection to the physical world and the society they inhabit. In this case, Waifs' claims of "delusions" or "being delusional" is comprarable to divine messages from God. The asceticism of nuns and saints also relates to this community's emphasis on anorexia as a form of "purity." Saint Catherine of Siena, who refused to eat anything but the Eucharist for the final years of her life, is popular for this reason exactly. Other popular religious figures in this community are Saint Joan of Arc, Saint Teresa of Avila, Mary Magdalene, and the Mother Mary Herself.

Ideas and imagery from New Age spirituality co-exist with the community's focus on Catholicism. Waif's idealization of manifestation (using intention to change reality), especially through subliminal videos (where videos montages set to music include implanted subliminal messages of manifestation), angel numbers, zodiac signs, intuition, and auras is a result of this.

Waifs are notoriously misanthropic, believing that most people are inferior and undesirable to them as friends or romantic partners. Waifs can feel uniquely misunderstood and special, both lonely but choosing to be alone due to their negative opinion of others. Many Waifs feel smarter, more aware (both of themselves and of the world around them/reality), more beautiful, and more troubled than the common person. Though they perform the trope of "man eater" (heavily tied to the "female manipulator" title), Waif memes often portray themselves as lacking friends or significant others. Depression, detachment, and general toxicity would ward off traditional relationships with healthy individuals. This is one reason why another term for this aesthetic is "Femcel." Many memes and Whisper posts reference being chronically online, hating conversation, and feeling alienated from their peers -- these are traits they share with the Incel community. Though Waifs may struggle with social connection, most are not femcels in the true sense of the term, but rather claim the title because it's provocative, creating an edge that contrasts with the traditionally feminine aesthetic.

The community embraces themes of neuroticism and mental illness. Many works in the Waif canon focuses on protagonists who feature symptoms of mental illness, and Girlbloggers often find them relatable and strive to be like them despite (or because of) their personality flaws and poor relationships. There is also a facetious longing for lobotomies, creating the overlap with Lobotomy Chic.

Openly advertising toxic traits in this community is part of a larger trend online, especially on TikTok and Whisper. Candidly discussing being narcissistic, dishonest, unstable, and manipulative is considered a demonstration of authenticity, and contrasts starkly with more mainstream values of "toxic positivity" and mental wellness. This, of course, has a gendered component: traditionally, women are encouraged to be kind and outwardly focused. Openly displaying "unlikable" traits rejects this standard, and is tied to an increase of women-written media which portrays the realities of women as individuals, rather than a feminine ideal.

Inadvertently, this has led to the community's sympathy for women deemed insane, cruel, or evil. Two figures often discussed in Girlblogging spheres are Amy Dunne and Jodi Arias, both who hurt their romantic partners. Though Dunne is a fictional character, Jodi Arias is not, and despite the real-world harm Arias caused, she is idolized all the same. Some in the community claim that both women were justified in carrying out their crimes because of the slights they experienced in their lives; this is said with a twinge of facetiousness.

Overall, the Girlblogger persona is one steeped in irony, self-awareness, and self-deprecation, with direct references to the concepts of personae, the hyperreal, the male gaze, and more; it is incredibly layered and nuanced, and yet simultaneously superficial and vapid. All of this is acknowledged and celebrated within the aesthetic.

The easiest way to spot an image from the Waif community is the format: an aesthetic photograph with some sort of text overtop. The image itself may be in the form of a collage or a single picture, the text is sometimes stylized (colored differently, or in a cursive/script font), and the photos are often edited with a pale filter. This trend is a remnant of the aesthetics' origins on the Whisper app, which formats "whispers" as text-on-images. The font used in the app is called Upright Regular. Now that Whisper has been defunct since 2025, most new Girlblogging images use script fonts instead. The color palette is often pale and pastel-oriented, with the most frequent being white, black and gray, pinks, soft blues, and brown. Background images typically comprise of one or more of the visuals detailed below.

A common visual is images of glamorous women who have "Waif energy" -- thin, beautiful, and often with a detached, intimidating or cold aura. Sometimes their expressions will seem sad or faraway; sometimes they look blasé or cheeky. Typically, they will be dressed in Waifish fashion as well. Oftentimes they are celebrities, either through Hollywood or on the internet, but sometimes they are just random, beautiful women -- in which case, they are meant to represent the viewer. Models, either on the runway or in candid photos with unprofessional lighting and grimy environments, musicians, and actresses are all typical subjects of a Waif image. Similarly, screencaps and gifs of movies within the Waif canon are also popular - these are movies that portray Waifs or Waif-like characters, such as the Virgin Suicides, Black Swan, Girl, Interrupted, and Pearl. Girlbloggers often find these characters relatable and aspirational.

Aside from models, fashion images are the next most popular subject. Runway details, designer storefronts, shopping bags, and cosmetics showcase the beauty of these girls and the aspirational lifestyle they have.

Another important visual is that of bedrooms, where Waifs spend most of their time. These bedroom photos have a range of looks. Some are messy and chaotic to the point of dysfunction, further relating the aesthetic to the popular Femcel NEET stereotype; some are sparse to the point of asceticism, with white as the only color, reminiscent of rooms in a psych ward or monastery. Often, there is a single cross on the wall. Another bedroom archetype leans more into the hyper-feminine, with lots of pink, feminine objects (stuffed animals, clothing, dolls, girly decor, etc.), often similar to Shabby Chic. And even furthermore, sometimes the room is decrepit and in disrepair, with peeling paint, decaying furniture, and dirty bedding. These aren't necessarily the real rooms of the Girlbloggers posting them, but are more so used to curate a vibe around their online persona.

Ballet is another important visual, specifically Russian ballet academies. Rather than images of performances with full costumes, however, these images always take place during class, independent practice, or downtime. Images that follow the "what's in my bag" trend for ballet students are also popular; these typically include visuals of pointe shoes, iPods, magazines, towels, etc. Non-dance related "what's in my bag" posts often show hair brushes, rosaries, books (within the Waif canon), plush keychains, jewelry, cigarettes, and perfumes.

Russian/Slavic culture is frequently referenced in fashion, literary tastes, Whisper posts, and through a fascination with the Slavic Dolls of the 2000s. This manifests in several ways, but most often through the idealized image of a stereotypical Slavic woman: conventionally attractive, thin, pale, blonde-haired, and blue-eyed. The fact that Waif darling Dasha Nekrasova is from Belarus contributes to this admiration.

There are frequent references to having cigarettes and black or iced coffee, common hunger suppressants utilized in pro-ana communities, as well as items associated with intellectualism and sophistication. Canned Diet Coke is another common photo subject and reference to anorexia. Cherry Coke is an alternative to this, a reference to Lana Del Rey's song "Cola." Schnapps and vodka, especially cherry-flavored, also refer to a Lana Del Rey song, "This is What Makes Us Girls," and relate to the Russia fixation and party lifestyle that these girls long for.

Catholicism and Catholic school imagery is also popular. Schoolgirls in uniform, nuns, saints, Bibles, and rosaries often appear as visuals. This is a part of a larger trend, as Catholic motifs have become more widespread in late 2021-early 2022 alternative fashion, with irony and sincerity being blurred. The religious imagery is often sacrilegious and ironic, contrasted between overt sexuality, drugs, and partying, and even sometimes going to full on Catholic Horror, similar to Morute.

Similarly, prep school in general is often referenced. Images of Rory Gilmore and other fictional characters or celebrities in school uniforms reading and holding books of high literary merit are common. Literature is generally celebrated, with books by Sylvia Plath, Anaïs Nin, Joan Didion, and the Brontë sisters appearing in many Waif images.

Another motif often used are prey animals, particularly fawns or lambs. They are often a visual representation of innocence and cuteness, but are also symbols of fragility and vulnerability. The importance of "doe eyes" in feminine looks also contributes to this link.

Edited screenshots of news articles from the digital magazines Vulture and The Cut are common, where, instead of a fashion/cultural title, the magazine would "report" on the mundane activities of a Girlblogger or model.

There are also multiple micro variations of this aesthetic, with users leaving out certain elements or adding in elements from Preppy, Pink Parisian, Morute, Downtown Girl, Babygirl, Messy French It Girl, Vintage Americana and more. The constant between all Waifs is their admiration for models, the shared language, and the memes.
For the purposes of citation and examples, see the Wayback Machine archive of the Tumblr tag.

Slogans and phrases are also incredibly crucial to this community, and are often repeated within posts or to each other as a way to connect themselves with the rest of the community. Some of them include:
"I'm like (toxic male fictional character, songs, objects, etc.) but a girl"
"In my (word salad, fictional character, songs, etc.) era"
"In a (word salad, fictional character, etc.) way"
"Esoteric" as a way of describing themselves, typically in reference to spirituality, niche book and film taste, etc.
"This is what makes us girls," a reference to the Lana Del Rey song of the same name.
[Blank] girl autumn/winter, a variation on the phrase "Christian girl autumn," which itself is a variation on "Hot girl summer."
Phrases that address a girl (the viewer) directly, such as "girl help", "girl whatever," etc.
"Rotting," referring to being unproductive and inactive in bed, aka "bed rotting."
References to "The Joker," the Batman villain who, in the 2019 film, snaps and becomes a mass-murderer after a life of mental illness and social ostracization.
Another defining feature of the Waif community are its niche memes. Memes include:

"I would go to school if..." followed by a series of photos and captions: "if this were the teacher" beneath Waif icons, "if this was the uniform" beneath examples of Waif fashion, and "if this was the lunch" beneath Waif-related food and drink.
"If this is her vibe, RUN" (or some variation) overlaid on a collage of Waif imagery.
"This is me, if you even care," over an image of a beautiful character, innocent creature, cute doll, etc., representing the vibe the poster wishes to exude.
"When your circle small but all y'all crazy!" (or some variation) text overlaid on an image of several Waif-related figures, fictional or real.

"Boys' pockets versus girls' pockets;" beneath the "boy's pockets" label will be one or two standard objects (typically just keys and a phone), while the "girl's pockets" label will have a plethora of aesthetic-related objects.
"Me as a perfume..." where perfume notes (top note, middle notes, base notes) being replaced with objects that represent the vibe of the poster.
"Girlhood is a spectrum," captioned above two contrasting images.

Another way of participating in the online community is through comment/tag games, also known as "What vibe do I give off?" posts, where a series of Waif-related images are presented in labelled rows. The goal is for the Girlblogger to pick one item from each row which describe her best, or to send the post to her friends and have them tell her which items describe her best.

Moodboards are another common way of engaging in Girlblogger spheres. Images of Waifish clothes are collected into a collage alongside other Waif-related imagery and phrases in an attempt to curate the vibe/persona of the poster.

An additional meme within the community is relating yourself to Franz Kafka or his infamous character, the protagonist of The Metamorphosis. In Kafka's novella, a man is transformed into a giant bug overnight (often visually represented as a cockroach), symbolizing the loneliness, alienation, and dehumanization he experiences in his normal life. Waifs relate to this experience as well as to the author himself, who often explored these themes in his work.
Of course, this isn't an exhaustive list of every meme and joke format within the community, and many more exist in online Girlblogger spaces. Some more examples will be displayed below.

Waif fashion largely originates from the hyper-feminine luxury fashion of the 2000s McBling aesthetic, the original Dark Nymphet aesthetic, and trends of the early 2020s such as Coquette, Dollette and Balletcore. The styling can range from being prim and polished to messy and disorganized, tailored to the specific Waifs' persona. The through line that connects it all together is the emphasis on skinniness, which is seen as aspirational to those without it and as a status symbol for those with it. One way this is shown is through wearing Brandy Melville, a brand known for having "one-size-fits-all" clothing that only fits on thin, petite women.

The garments that are based on 2000s trends, such as low-rise jeans and baby tees, are deliberately skimpy to emphasize the fact that the wearer can do so without being perceived as "unflattering" or "inappropriate" (due to their thinness).
A common motif is screenprinting Waif visuals onto clothes, particularly baby tees. This is often done by small, independent businesses on Depop or Instagram.

As mentioned before, media is an important aspect of this aesthetic. Literary works, films, television shows, and music are all referenced often, through quotes and as screenshots and GIFs. It is also a means for Waifs to connect with each other; Girlbloggers bond over shared media interests, and the content that is within the Waif "canon" is an easy way for girls in this aesthetic to identify and relate to one another. Media also serves as inspiration for fashion, visuals, phrases, and values.

The Waif canon is a list of publications that are extremely important to the Waif aesthetic. These are movies, shows, and songs that nearly every Waif has seen/heard directly, or has seen/heard references to within the community. Many of these works include themes of mental illness, traumatic events, or disordered personalities. Because of this, most of them are in the psychological drama or psychological horror genres. The protagonists of these stories are often feminine women with relatively privileged positions in life who, nevertheless, experience suffering due to their mental illnesses, poor relationships, or behavioral issues. Sometimes, they are in a toxic entanglement with a male love interest or close female friend.

Visually, these works may or may not resemble each other or the Waif aesthetic. For example, the Joker is often referenced, but not due to his aesthetic or visual appeal -- more so due to the relatability of his instability and suffering. Conversely, many of the works in the Waif canon have become popular solely for the aesthetics rather than for the motifs, such as Marie Antoinette (2006), whose hyper-feminine visuals are often used as the background images in posts.

There also exists an extension into philosophical literature and poetry, a commonality this aesthetic has with Thought Daughter. Though not canonized in the same way the music or fiction is, these works are still relevant and are sometimes discussed in Waif spheres or on Waif-related podcasts like Red Scare.

The Chic Diet by Kit Olsen
Girl in Pieces by Kathleen Glasgow
How to Murder Your Life by Cat Marnell
My Year of Rest and Relaxation by Ottessa Moshfegh
The Secret History by Donna Tartt

The Waif community prioritizes music by and for women due to its innate relatability with their lived experience. The three popular genres are 2010s indie pop, 90s-2000s rock and alt rock, and 2020s indie rock and dream pop. Within the first grouping, you will see many artists popularized during the rise of the 2010s Tumblr Soft Grunge and Sadgirl aesthetics. The connection that runs through all three types is the focus on woman-led vocals and lyrics, though there are a few notable exceptions (such as the Smiths, Nirvana, and Deftones).

The Girlblogging community primarily centers itself around two activities: internet posting (girlblogging) and bedrotting. Not mutually exclusive to one another, bedrotting refers to spending all day in bed, typically on your phone, due to depression, stress, or social exhaustion. Other Waif hobbies include reading literature and philosophy, watching films, listening to music, shopping, thrifting, going to cafes, vlogging, and photography.
Girlbloggers also love to journal and create moodboards, sometimes even venturing into scrapbooking or collaging.

New Age spirituality/teen girl pseudoscience has led to an increased interest in manifestation, particularly through subliminal videos, as well as yoga, meditation, affirmations, and engaging in astrology. Physical activities that Waifs sometimes participate in include ballet and barre exercises, pilates, and going on "hot girl walks" (walking outdoors while thinking affirmations).

Some Waifs who identify more strongly with the "femcel" title will engage in looksmaxxing and public venting, usually through online spaces such as the FemaleDatingStrategy, GirlDinnerDiaries, HowToBeHot, TheGirlSurvivalGuide and Vindicta Reddit communities.

The aesthetic is not remiss of criticism. The most prevalent criticism is of the pro-ana or thinspo elements. As previously noted, thinness and the idolization of thinness are key aspects to the community. Much of Waif imagery can be triggering to those who are currently in the process of overcoming eating disorders, and the community's obsession with weight as a whole is considered to be unhealthy to those outside of it. Additionally, the aesthetic has a pretty homogeneous image, tending to prefer imagery of thin white woman more so than any other demographic. Waifs also sometimes face criticism for their connection to Coquette and its Lolita romanticization. Many believe that the desire to be thin and frail stems from pedophilic beauty standards, and the glorification of youth (especially the teenage years) is an extension of that.

Others, especially Tumblr veterans, simply find this community annoying. Its formulaic visuals and meme formats are seen as repetitive, and the overusage of tags (unrelated to the images) and word salads are seen as nonsensical and juvenile. Some fans of the media pieces that are within the Waif canon dislike this community because of their co-optation of said pieces, believing that Waifs misinterpret these works, to the detriment of the artist's intent and the perception of the fan bases.
"The Birth of the Girlblogger" (2023) by Savannah Bradley
"Intimacy and the Machine: Slouching Towards Girlblogging" (2022) by Biz Sherbert
